facts.title: A three-way photo finish
facts.text: Boron was first isolated in 1808, almost simultaneously by the French chemists Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thenard in Paris and the Englishman Humphry Davy in London. None of them obtained it very pure, getting samples only around 50% boron. The element was not produced in high purity until 1909, when the American chemist Ezekiel Weintraub made it about 99% pure.

facts.title: Named after a desert mineral
facts.text: The name boron comes from borax, a mineral known for centuries and used as a flux and cleaning agent, blended with the ending of carbon because boron resembled it. Borax itself traces to the Arabic word buraq and the Persian burah. So the element is essentially named after the salty white powder it was first extracted from.

facts.title: The cosmic outsider
facts.text: Boron is one of the rarest light elements in the universe because it is not made inside stars the way carbon or oxygen are. Instead it forms mostly through cosmic ray spallation, when high-energy particles racing through space smash heavier nuclei like carbon and oxygen apart. This explains why boron is roughly a million times rarer in the cosmos than carbon despite sitting right beside it.

facts.title: Harder than you would guess
facts.text: Boron is a metalloid that behaves much more like a hard, brittle nonmetal than a metal. Crystalline boron is one of the hardest known elements, scoring around 9.3 on the Mohs scale, placing it just below diamond. Its compound boron nitride can be arranged into a cubic form that rivals diamond as a cutting and grinding abrasive.

facts.title: The neutron sponge
facts.text: The isotope boron-10, which makes up about 20 percent of natural boron, is exceptionally good at absorbing neutrons. This makes boron essential in nuclear reactors, where boron control rods and boric acid dissolved in the coolant soak up excess neutrons to control or shut down the chain reaction. The same property is used in radiation shielding and emergency reactor safety systems.

facts.title: It makes glass tough
facts.text: Adding boron oxide to glass produces borosilicate glass, which expands very little when heated and therefore resists cracking from sudden temperature changes. This is the science behind Pyrex cookware and most laboratory glassware that can go straight from a flame into cold water. Borosilicate glass is also used for the mirrors of large telescopes because it barely changes shape with temperature.

facts.title: A flash of brilliant green
facts.text: When boron compounds are heated in a flame, they burn with a vivid bright green color. Chemists use this green flame test as a quick way to detect the presence of boron in a sample. The same effect gives many green fireworks their color, often using compounds such as boric acid or borax.

facts.title: Quietly essential to plants
facts.text: Boron is a genuine micronutrient that plants cannot live without, even though they need only tiny amounts of it. It helps build and stabilize cell walls and is vital for flowering, pollination, and seed and fruit development. Boron-deficient soils cause real crop problems worldwide, so farmers often add boron-containing fertilizers to fields.

facts.title: Targeted cancer therapy
facts.text: A medical technique called boron neutron capture therapy uses boron-10 to attack tumors. Doctors deliver a boron compound that accumulates in cancer cells, then irradiate the area with low-energy neutrons. Each boron-10 nucleus that captures a neutron splits and releases tiny high-energy particles that destroy the nearby cancer cell while largely sparing healthy tissue around it.

facts.title: Mined from dry lakebeds
facts.text: Most of the world's boron is mined as borate minerals from ancient dried-up lakes in arid regions. The single richest source is the open-pit mine at Boron, California, in the Mojave Desert, while Turkey holds the largest reserves on Earth. These deposits formed when boron-rich waters from volcanic activity slowly evaporated over geological time.
